OIIX.name: FIR Tehran
OIIX.conflictType: Interstate conflict — Iran vs Israel/US (fragile ceasefire)
OIIX.narrative: EASA's CZIB-2026-04 reflects a ceasefire that has held since April 2026 but remains fragile, with an elevated Iranian air-defence posture that raises the risk of civil aircraft being misidentified. EASA has warned escalation could resume with little notice. The eastern part of the FIR was partially reopened for overflights in June 2026 while the western part remains closed; however, EASA continues to advise operators not to operate in the OIIX/Tehran FIR at any altitude. The shoot-down of Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran in Jan 2020 illustrates how quickly misidentification can prove fatal.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Very few international operators are using Iranian airspace; most Europe-Asia traffic routes south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 Iran has previously conducted missile activity close to busy international routes with little warning to civil aviation. Several states continue to warn against operations in Iranian airspace. Major events: July 2026: EASA's current CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate in the OIIX/Tehran FIR at any altitude following renewed military activity. June 2026: Iran partially reopened the eastern part of the OIIX/Tehran FIR for overflights; western part remains closed. March 2026: OIIX/Tehran FIR closed following large-scale US and Israeli strikes on Iranian military targets and subsequent Iranian missile and drone retaliation across the Middle East. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings and avoidance. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other, leading most international operators to avoid both airspaces. Jan 2020: Iran shot down Ukraine International Airlines flight 752 over Tehran after misidentifying the aircraft as a hostile target.

ORBB.name: FIR Baghdad
ORBB.conflictType: Non-state armed groups (IBMGs) + Iranian missile/drone spillover
ORBB.narrative: Despite the regional ceasefire, EASA cites recurrent Iranian drone and ballistic-missile strikes reaching Iraqi airspace, alongside the continued presence of Iranian-backed militant groups (IBMGs), as reasons the Baghdad FIR remains a do-not-operate zone. The FIR reopened to overflights in June 2026 following the US-Iran ceasefire, with north-south routes available, but EASA continues to advise operators not to operate at any altitude. Risks include missile and drone activity, misidentification by air-defence systems operated by local and foreign military forces, and MANPADS held by terrorist groups.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Iraqi airspace (the ORBB/Baghdad FIR) remains open to overflights and some operators continue using it; most Europe-Asia traffic still routes south via Egypt/Saudi or north via the Caucasus/Afghanistan. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 Several states continue to maintain airspace warnings for Iraq, and EASA continues to advise operators not to operate in the ORBB/Baghdad FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Major events: July 2026: EASA's current CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate in the ORBB/Baghdad FIR at any altitude. June 2026: ORBB/Baghdad FIR reopened to overflights following the US-Iran ceasefire, with north-south routes available. March 2026: ORBB/Baghdad FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation across the region. June 2025: Airspace closed following Israeli missile attack on Iran; missiles and drones transited Iraqi airspace. Apr 2024: Airspace closed due to Iran drone and missile strike on Israel. Apr 2023: Several drone and missile attacks in northern Iraq launched from Turkey and Iran, including strikes near ORSU and ORER. Oct 2021: US operators permitted to overfly the ORBB/Baghdad FIR above FL320 under updated FAA restrictions.

OLBB.name: FIR Beirut
OLBB.narrative: A Trilateral Framework Agreement between Israel, Lebanon and the US (26 June 2026) is a step toward consolidating the ceasefire, but EASA notes its long-term implementation is uncertain, and that Lebanon has not shown it can proactively manage airspace risk. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continued through February–July 2026 despite repeated ceasefire extensions. Some states allow limited operations to OLBA/Beirut provided arrivals and departures remain over the Mediterranean Sea. GNSS spoofing and jamming have been reported in the OLBB/Beirut FIR since November 2023.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military activity around the Strait of Hormuz. Israeli airstrikes in Lebanon continue and most international operators continue to avoid the airspace. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is military activity linked to the Israel-Hezbollah conflict and the wider regional security situation, including missile and drone activity. Several states maintain long-standing warnings advising operators to avoid Lebanese airspace, and EASA continues to advise operators not to operate in the OLBB/Beirut FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Major events: July 2026: EASA's current CZIB continues to advise operators not to operate in the OLBB/Beirut FIR at any altitude following renewed military activity in the region. Feb-Jul 2026: Israeli airstrikes continued in Lebanon despite repeated ceasefire extensions and diplomatic efforts. Oct 2024: Israel launched a ground operation against Hezbollah in southern Lebanon. Nov 2023 - ongoing: GNSS spoofing and jamming reported in the OLBB/Beirut FIR.

OJAC.name: FIR Amman
OJAC.conflictType: Missile/drone overflight risk (regional spillover, no direct conflict on Jordanian soil)
OJAC.narrative: Jordan's airspace has repeatedly seen Iranian missiles and drones pass through en route to other targets, intercepted by Jordanian and allied air defences. Jordanian authorities have not published any airspace restrictions of their own despite this activity. The OJAC/Amman FIR remains open and operating normally; EASA has issued an Information Note advising operators to factor the potential risk into their planning.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Jordan airspace (the OJAC/Amman FIR) remains open and is operating normally. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is missile and drone activity linked to regional conflicts. Jordan has previously been affected by missiles and drones crossing its airspace during escalations involving Israel and Iran. EASA's current Information Note advises operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new Information Note advising operators to take the potential risk into account before operating in the OJAC/Amman FIR following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb-Jul 2026: Jordan remained open throughout the Iran conflict, although missile and drone activity affected several neighbouring countries. Apr 2024: Jordan temporarily closed its airspace during the Iranian drone and missile attack on Israel. Oct 2023: Jordan intercepted drones and missiles transiting its airspace during regional escalation.

OKAC.name: FIR Kuwait
OKAC.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OKAC.narrative: Kuwait hosts major US military facilities, making it a plausible target for Iranian retaliation and increasing the risk of civil aircraft being caught up in an attack or an air-defence response. Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport in March 2026. The FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict and is currently open for arrivals and departures only; overflights remain prohibited. EASA advises operators not to operate in the OKAC/Kuwait FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Kuwait has been directly affected by the conflict; the OKAC/Kuwait FIR is currently open for arrivals and departures only — overflights remain prohibited. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is missile and drone activity linked to the wider Iran conflict. EASA advises operators not to operate in the OKAC/Kuwait FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate in the OKAC/Kuwait FIR at any altitude following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb-Jul 2026: OKAC/Kuwait FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict; currently open for arrivals and departures only. March 2026: Missile and drone strikes damaged OKKK/Kuwait airport. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes across the region.

OBBB.name: FIR Bahrain
OBBB.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OBBB.narrative: As with Kuwait and Qatar, the US military presence in Bahrain is the main driver of EASA's risk assessment for this FIR. The OBBB/Bahrain FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to normal overflight operations; Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states in March 2026, with incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. EASA advises operators not to operate in the FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Bahrain airspace (the OBBB/Bahrain FIR) remains open to overflights. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is missile and drone activity linked to the wider Iran conflict. Bahrain lies close to several key military facilities in the Gulf region. EASA advises operators not to operate in the OBBB/Bahrain FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate in the OBBB/Bahrain FIR at any altitude following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb-Jul 2026: OBBB/Bahrain FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before reopening to normal overflight operations. March 2026: Iranian missile and drone attacks targeted several Gulf states, including incidents affecting airspace around Bahrain. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OTDF.name: FIR Doha
OTDF.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OTDF.narrative: Qatar hosts significant US forces and has itself been targeted by Iranian strikes during the recent escalation, keeping it on EASA's do-not-operate list even as operational conditions ease. An Iranian missile strike was reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha in March 2026. The OTDF/Doha FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before returning to largely normal operations; EASA advises operators not to operate at any altitude under its current CZIB.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Qatar airspace (the OTDF/Doha FIR) remains open and is operating largely normally. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is missile and drone activity linked to the wider Iran conflict. Qatar was directly affected during the conflict, including missile strikes near Doha. EASA advises operators not to operate in the OTDF/Doha FIR at any altitude under its current CZIB. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate in the OTDF/Doha FIR at any altitude following renewed military activity in the Gulf. Feb-Jul 2026: OTDF/Doha FIR closed and reopened several times during the Iran conflict before reopening to normal overflight operations. March 2026: Iranian missile strike reported at Al Udeid Air Base near Doha. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the region.

OMAE.name: FIR Emirates
OMAE.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OMAE.narrative: The UAE's proximity to the Strait of Hormuz and its role as a regional hub keep it firmly within EASA's risk assessment, despite being operationally busy.

OOMM.name: FIR Muscat — west of 58°E only
OOMM.conflictType: Interstate tension — Iran vs US (Strait of Hormuz)
OOMM.narrative: Unlike other Gulf FIRs, only the western portion of Omani/Gulf of Oman waters is covered — reflecting where commercial vessel attacks and Strait of Hormuz tension actually concentrate. Oman remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route (Egypt-Saudi-Oman) used by operators avoiding the closed central Middle East corridor. EASA advises operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Oman airspace (the OOMM/Muscat FIR) remains open and carries significant Europe-Asia overflight traffic as a key part of the southern bypass route. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 The primary risk is spillover of missile or drone activity from conflicts elsewhere in the region. EASA's current CZIB advises operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E. Major events: July 2026: EASA issued a new CZIB advising operators not to operate over the waters of the Gulf of Oman within the OOMM/Muscat FIR west of 58°E. Feb-Jul 2026: Oman remained open throughout the Iran conflict and became a key part of the main southern bypass route. June 2025: Israel and Iran exchanged missile strikes, prompting renewed airspace warnings across the Gulf region. Oct 2024: Israel and Iran carried out missile attacks against each other, leading many operators to avoid airspace between the two countries.

OSTT.name: FIR Damascus
OSTT.narrative: EASA's longest-running Middle East bulletin (19 revisions since 2017) reflects a still-unresolved multi-actor conflict. Traffic patterns have shifted: OSTT quietly reopened to some regional carriers in early 2025 as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq corridor, even though most Western operators continue to avoid it. The primary risks are military activity linked to the Syria conflict, Israeli airstrikes targeting Iranian and Hezbollah-linked positions, and the potential for misidentification by air-defence systems.

cross.detail: July 2026: The US-Iran ceasefire has effectively broken down, with renewed military action and attacks around the Strait of Hormuz. Syrian airspace (the OSTT/Damascus FIR) remains high risk, but some regional operators have started using it again as an alternative to the more restricted Iran/Iraq routing. See OPSGROUP Briefing : Middle East airspace situation - 2026 Several countries continue to prohibit or advise against operations in the OSTT/Damascus FIR due to the risk from military operations, anti-aviation weaponry and unstable security conditions. Major events: March 2026: OSTT/Damascus FIR closed following US and Israeli strikes on Iran and subsequent Iranian retaliation across the region. Jan-Jul 2026: A gradual increase in overflights through Syria as some regional operators use the FIR as an alternative to Iran and Iraq. Dec 2024: Syrian airspace temporarily closed following the fall of the Assad regime. Oct 2023: Airstrikes damaged runways at OSDI/Damascus and OSAP/Aleppo airports. Feb 2020: An A320 approaching Damascus diverted after being caught in crossfire during Israeli airstrikes. Sep 2018: Russian IL-20 shot down in error near the Syria-Cyprus FIR boundary.

OYSC.name: FIR Sana'a only
OYSC.conflictType: Civil war + interstate spillover (Red Sea attacks)
OYSC.narrative: This bulletin covers only the Sana'a FIR, not the whole of Yemen. The ongoing civil war and Houthi involvement in the wider regional conflict keep the risk assessment unchanged since 2017.

cross.detail: Yemen remains an active conflict zone, and the vast majority of Yemeni airspace (OYSC/Sanaa FIR) should be avoided. Several countries prohibit aircraft from overflying any land portion of the FIR. US operators can still use offshore routes UT702 and M999, while other countries permit flights on overwater portions of Yemeni airspace. Saudi airspace to the north and Somali airspace to the south also have risks. The primary risk is intentional targeting by terrorist groups with access to sophisticated anti-aircraft weaponry. Civil aircraft may also be at risk from ongoing high-intensity military operations including explosive drones and missiles. Saudi and Israeli airstrikes can occur at any time, including in the capital Sana'a. Major events: Jul 2026: Yemen's government carried out an airstrike on the runway at OYSN/Sanaa Airport to stop an Iranian aircraft from landing. Dec 2024 - ongoing: OYSN/Sanaa Airport closed due to damage from Israeli airstrikes in Dec 2024 and May 2025. Jan 2024: US and UK carried out airstrikes against Houthi rebels in Yemen, in response to recent missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea. Sep 2023: Houthi drone attacks near the Yemen-Saudi border. Apr-Oct 2022: All parties in the Yemeni conflict agreed a ceasefire. 2018-2022: Frequent Saudi airstrikes on Sanaa and other targets in Yemen in retaliation for Houthi drone attacks across the border. 2017: OYSN/Sanaa Airport badly damaged by coalition airstrikes. Saudi-Yemen Airspace Update, Oct 2020 (OPSGROUP article)

UUWV.name: FIR Moscow and others (west of 60°E)
UUWV.conflictType: Interstate war — Russian invasion of Ukraine (air-defence risk)
UUWV.narrative: Issued after the likely accidental shoot-down of Azerbaijan Airlines flight 8243 near Grozny in December 2024, this bulletin reflects the risk that Russian air-defence systems responding to Ukrainian strikes pose to civil aircraft, compounded by widespread GNSS interference. Drone attacks across Russia have been ramping up, with some reaching as far as Siberia, increasing risk for any aircraft using Russian airspace. Russian air-defence systems use surface-to-air missiles capable of reaching all altitudes, so the risk applies at every flight level.

cross.detail: As of June 2025, drone attacks across Russia are ramping up, with some reaching as far as Siberia. Hundreds of drones have been shot down recently, including in areas around Moscow. Russian air-defence systems are using surface-to-air missiles capable of reaching all altitudes, so the risk applies at every level. Most operators avoid Russian airspace completely; those still flying there should be prepared for sudden closures or reroutes. Most activity happens at night, but daytime disruptions are now common. Ukraine's airspace has remained fully closed to civil aviation since the Russian invasion in Feb 2022. Several countries continue to prohibit their operators from using Russian airspace near the FIR boundaries with Ukraine. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military systems near the Russia-Ukraine border, including misidentification (as with MAS17, UIA752). Major events: Jan 2025: EASA issued a new CZIB recommending against flights in Western Russia (anywhere west of 60 deg E) due to the threat of anti-aircraft fire and high danger of misidentification by air-defence systems targeting Ukrainian drones and missiles. This follows the shoot-down of a passenger jet at URMG/Grozny on Dec 25. Jan 2024: Crash of military transport aircraft in Russian airspace near Belgarod, approx 20nm from the Ukrainian border. Both Russia and Ukraine accused each other of shooting it down. Aug 2023: The private jet carrying Wagner mercenary chief Yevgeny Prigozhin crashed en route from Moscow to St Petersburg on Aug 23. July 2023 - ongoing: Several incidents of drone strikes on targets in Moscow and surrounding region, with some drones damaging buildings and Moscow airports being forced to close temporarily on many occasions. These events are becoming more frequent inside Russian airspace. OPSGROUP article: Ukraine and Russia Update March 2022

UKBV.name: All Ukrainian FIRs
UKBV.narrative: In force since the day of the invasion, this remains one of the clearest and most stable prohibitions in this dataset — Ukraine itself has closed its FIRs to civil traffic by NOTAM.

cross.detail: Ukraine closed its entire airspace to all civil traffic on Feb 24, 2022, due to a military invasion by Russia. There is an ongoing active conflict in Ukraine between Russian and Ukrainian forces. Russia, Belarus and Moldova have closed large sections of their own airspace near to their FIR boundaries with Ukraine. All the major countries who regularly issue airspace warnings (the US, UK, Canada, France, Germany, Italy) have since issued total flight bans for Ukraine due to risk from military activity at all levels. The primary risk is unintended targeting of civil aircraft by military, including misidentification (as with MAS17, UIA752), or confusion. The secondary risk is potential lack of Ukrainian Air Traffic Control Service at short notice (cyber attack), and other unforeseeable non-normal operating environments for civil aircraft. OPSGROUP article: Ukraine and Russia Update March 2022 Prior to February 2022, there were two areas of concern in Ukraine — the conflict in the far east of the country (affecting UKDV/Dnipro FIR) and the double claim over ATC and airspace in Crimea (UKFV/URFV/Simferopol FIR).

HSSS.name: FIR Khartoum
HSSS.conflictType: Civil war — Sudan Armed Forces (SAF) vs Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
HSSS.narrative: The ongoing SAF–RSF civil war has put anti-aircraft artillery, MANPADS and SAM systems into play across the whole of Sudanese airspace, keeping the entire Khartoum FIR off-limits. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed though no NOTAMs are being issued; a contingency plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. The primary risk on the ground concerns unplanned diversions, with reports of passenger jets being targeted by gunfire at HSSK/Khartoum airport throughout the conflict.

cross.detail: Following a military coup in April 2023, Sudan remains closed to all civilian flights. In South Sudan, air navigation services remain suspended above FL245. There is ongoing fighting in Sudan between government and militant forces. HSSK/Khartoum airport is closed, but no NOTAMs are being issued. A contingency plan with published overflight routes via HSPN/Port Sudan, Egypt, Saudi Arabia and South Sudan is available. Several countries have issued airspace warnings advising their operators not to enter Sudanese airspace due to risks from anti-aircraft weaponry and military activity. OPSGROUP article: Sudan Airspace Update, Nov 2025 The secondary risk relates to Sudan's proximity to South Sudan, which has poor levels of ATC provision for overflights below FL245. Major events: Nov 2025: Il-76 reportedly shot down by a surface-to-air missile near Babanusa, southern Sudan. May 2025: Drone attack targeting critical infrastructure including HSPN/Port Sudan airport. Oct 2024: Foreign-registered cargo aircraft was shot down by local militia over North Darfur (Western Sudan, near the border with Chad). Apr 2023: Military coup on Apr 15. Sudan's airspace closed, South Sudan's airspace closed above FL245. Oct 2021: Military coup on Oct 25. HSSK/Khartoum airport closed for two days, with all flights suspended.

HLLL.name: FIR Tripoli
HLLL.narrative: Libya's two rival governments and various non-state armed actors create a real risk of misidentification when crossing between areas controlled by different authorities. The one carve-out is for coastal airport approaches made from over the sea. Reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed, with regular ATS and radar outages across the HLLL FIR and severe limitations in VHF capability.
HLLL.restrictionLabel: Do not operate, except flights to coastal airports approached from the sea, subject to ATC contact and your own risk assessment

cross.detail: A civil war has been ongoing since 2014. Some progress was made in Oct 2020 with the formation of a new government, but Libya remains an active conflict zone with armed clashes between rival militia groups. Total flight ban for US operators; several other countries have warnings in place. The primary risk is misidentification by Libyan air-defence systems, or by militia who have threatened to shoot down aircraft operating in western Libya, including at HLLM/Tripoli Mitiga airport. Military activity is reported over the high seas, either operating as OAT or not in contact with ATC. The secondary risk is that reliable ATC services cannot be guaranteed, with regular ATS and radar outages across the HLLL FIR and severe VHF limitations, requiring operators to communicate with Malta ATC for guidance. Libya Airspace Update, Feb 2024 (OPSGROUP article) Major events: August 2023: Major evacuation of aircraft from Tripoli due to violent clashes and gunfire at Mitiga airport. Tripoli mass evacuation of aircraft (OPSGROUP article) July 2023: Italy cancelled its 10-year ban on flights to/from Libya. Aug 2022: Militia air-defence forces claimed to have shot down a US drone operating in the vicinity of Benghazi. June 2022: Failed militia attempt to seize Tripoli government offices resulted in armed clashes and suspension of flights at HLLM/Mitiga airport. Jan 2020: Multiple airstrikes targeting HLLM/Mitiga airport. Nov 2019: Militia advancing on Tripoli declared a no-fly-zone around the city, threatening to shoot down civil aircraft attempting to fly to HLLM/Mitiga airport. 2014: HLLT/Tripoli airport closed after clashes between rival militias destroyed most of the airport's facilities; most flights now operate out of HLLM/Mitiga airport.

DRRR.name: Malian territory, especially the north-east
DRRR.conflictType: Insurgency — non-state armed groups active across the Sahel
DRRR.narrative: Non-state armed groups operating in Mali, particularly in the north-east, are assessed to have MANPADS and SAM missile capability, which is why the restriction is altitude-based rather than a total ban. ATS in Mali is provided by the GOOO/Dakar and DRRR/Niamey FIRs, which maintain a long-standing restriction for overflights of Mali to published ATS routes at FL320 and above. The security situation escalated sharply in April 2026, with coordinated attacks nationwide and sporadic fighting ongoing near GABS/Bamako.

cross.detail: The conflict in northern and central Mali has continued since 2012 and the security situation remains volatile. Several countries have airspace warnings in place, typically advising operations at or above FL250 or FL260 and avoiding GATB/Timbuktu, GAGO/Gao and GAKL/Kidal. The US advises caution in Mali airspace at all levels due to ongoing fighting, expanding militant activity, and the presence of a state-run paramilitary force operating anti-aircraft systems, military aircraft, UAS and electronic warfare equipment. The primary risks include MANPADS and other surface-to-air weapons, indirect fire near airports, and the potential for misidentification or spillover from military activity. Low-level and airport-phase operations carry the highest exposure. More info can be found in this ASECNA AIP SUP. Major events: April 2026: The security situation escalated sharply. On April 25, multiple armed groups carried out coordinated attacks nationwide against state and military targets, with gunfire and explosions reported near GABS/Bamako. Sporadic fighting is ongoing. France has issued a new airspace warning advising French operators not to operate to/from GABS or use it as an alternate. Sep 2024: Insurgents breached GABS/Bamako and set the presidential jet on fire; multiple attacks occurred across the city and the airport closed temporarily. Dec 2023: Germany prohibited its operators below FL260 in northern Mali due to escalating militant activity. Commercial flights to GATB/Timbuktu were cancelled after shelling near the airport; a military jet crashed near GAGO/Gao the same day, with reports it may have been shot down. Aug 2020: All airports closed for two days during a military coup; Bamako ACC remained operational and overflights were unaffected. Apr 2018: Militants attacked UN bases near GATB/Timbuktu using indirect fire and vehicle bombs. Jan 2017 and Nov 2016: Vehicle bomb and rocket attacks targeted GAGO/Gao and GATB/Timbuktu airports.

HCSM.name: Somali airspace
HCSM.conflictType: Insurgency — Al-Shabaab and related terrorist groups
HCSM.narrative: Terrorist organisations operating in Somalia are assessed to have confirmed anti-aircraft weaponry, possibly including MANPADS, driving the same FL260 altitude floor as Mali. An authority dispute in the north of the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR has added a further complication: from November 2025, Somaliland has required a PPR from its own CAA for all overflights, while Somalia has reaffirmed through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR — operators should expect conflicting permit instructions near Hargeisa and northern Somalia.

cross.detail: The central government has little control of the major cities and ports, with ongoing attacks from extremist militants showing an intent to target aviation interests. The primary risk is to overflying aircraft at the lower flight levels, which may be targeted by anti-aircraft-capable weapons. The US prohibits flights across Somalia's airspace (the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR) below FL260 except for flights transiting the overwater portion going to/from HDAM/Djibouti airport. Several other countries have issued airspace warnings advising against operating below FL260. The secondary risk is from aircraft being contacted by unauthorised ATC units issuing climb/descent instructions that conflict with official ones from Mogadishu Control. There is also an authority dispute in the north of the FIR: from Nov 2025, Somaliland has required a PPR from its own CAA for all overflights, while Somalia has reaffirmed through an AIC that it controls the entire FIR. Major events: Feb 2024: OPSGROUP received several reports of aircraft within the Mogadishu FIR being contacted by a 'fake controller' on the same frequency, issuing conflicting instructions. Aug 2023: Reports of uncontrolled operations including combat helicopters flying at low levels (FL030) not reporting position, altitude or routing. Oct 2022: The Somalian government warned that HCMM/Mogadishu airport may be targeted by militant groups amid escalating conflict. May 2022: Class A airspace implemented in the HCSM/Mogadishu FIR above FL245. 2020-ongoing: Multiple instances of Al-Shabaab attacks on HCMM/Mogadishu and nearby targets, including a UN compound. May 2020: An Embraer EMB-120 was shot down while on approach to Bardale airstrip, killing all six people on board — an accidental shoot-down by Ethiopian forces stationed in the region to combat Al-Shabaab.

OPKR.name: Baluchistan province (partial)
OPKR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPKR.narrative: Violent non-state actor (VNSA) groups with confirmed MANPADS operate in Baluchistan. The Kashmir dispute separately raises misidentification risk further north. In May 2025 there were four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in the Kashmir region; a ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held but the situation remains fragile. Current guidance generally advises operators to remain at or above FL260.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. In May 2025 there was a period of intense cross-border shelling and aerial activity in Kashmir. A ceasefire has largely held since then, but the situation remains fragile. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions rather than full avoidance, generally advising operators to remain at or above FL260. The primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry including the potential availability of MANPADS, particularly below FL260, as well as inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated. No new airspace closures or overflight bans issued; commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR, including via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in the Kashmir region. A ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held. Some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan, highlighting cross-border military activity risk. Dec 2023 - ongoing: Crew reports of GPS spoofing began emerging in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region, including airstrikes on both sides.

OPLR.name: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa province (partial)
OPLR.conflictType: Insurgency (violent non-state actors) + Kashmir territorial dispute
OPLR.narrative: Covers the north-western province, where the Kashmir dispute adds a misidentification risk on top of the VNSA activity common to both restricted Pakistani provinces. GPS spoofing has been reported in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore, since December 2023.

cross.detail: Tensions between Pakistan and India in the disputed Kashmir region, along with longstanding militant activity in parts of western Pakistan, create an ongoing risk in the OPKR/Karachi and OPLR/Lahore FIRs. In May 2025 there was a period of intense cross-border shelling and aerial activity in Kashmir. A ceasefire has largely held since then, but the situation remains fragile. Several states and EASA maintain altitude-based restrictions rather than full avoidance, generally advising operators to remain at or above FL260. The primary risks are from anti-aviation weaponry including the potential availability of MANPADS, particularly below FL260, as well as inadvertent risk from military activity or misidentification in the Kashmir region. Major events: Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated. No new airspace closures or overflight bans issued; commercial traffic continues to transit OAKX/Kabul FIR, including via P500 and G500. May 2025: Four days of cross-border strikes and shelling between India and Pakistan in the Kashmir region. A ceasefire announced on 10 May has largely held. Some operators temporarily rerouted south via the Gulf of Oman and UAE. Jan 2024: Iran conducted missile and drone strikes against a militant group in western Pakistan, highlighting cross-border military activity risk. Dec 2023 - ongoing: Crew reports of GPS spoofing began emerging in the OPLR/Lahore FIR area, particularly around OPLA/Lahore. Feb-Aug 2019: Pakistan closed its airspace to overflights following major clashes with India in the Kashmir region, including airstrikes on both sides.

OAKX.name: FIR Kabul
OAKX.conflictType: Post-conflict security vacuum — extremist groups active, limited air traffic services
OAKX.narrative: Since the 2021 Taliban takeover, Afghanistan has had little to no functioning air traffic control. The Kabul FIR is Class G airspace: crews use published contingency routes and TIBA procedures rather than normal ATC clearances. Traffic through the FIR increased in March 2026 as flights used the northern bypass route around the closed Middle East corridor following US and Israeli strikes on Iran. Some countries restrict overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the FIR; others allow overflights across the entire airspace at and above FL320.

cross.detail: March 2026: Afghanistan's airspace (OAKX/Kabul FIR) remains open but has no ATC service. The FIR is uncontrolled Class G airspace following the withdrawal of US and allied forces in Aug 2021. Traffic has increased recently as flights avoid the closed central Middle East corridor. See OPSGROUP Briefing : March 2026 - Afghanistan Overflight Update. Some countries restrict overflights to airways P500 and G500 in the far east of the OAKX/Kabul FIR; others allow overflights across the entire airspace at and above FL320. Overflights must be on specific contingency routes. The primary risk is from surface-to-air fire targeting aircraft at low altitudes. There is also no ATC service and an extreme threat to aircraft and crew safety and security on the ground. Major events: March 2026: Traffic increases through OAKX/Kabul FIR as flights use the northern bypass route around the closed Middle East corridor. Feb 2026: Cross-border strikes between Pakistan and Afghanistan escalated; commercial traffic continues to transit the FIR including via P500 and G500. Aug 2021: US and allied forces withdrew from Afghanistan; the OAKX/Kabul FIR became uncontrolled Class G airspace with no ATC service.

HAAA.name: FIR Addis Ababa, north of 8.5°N
HAAA.conflictType: Regional/border tension — assessed by EASA as medium risk
HAAA.narrative: This is an EASA Information Note, not a CZIB — meaning EASA's risk assessment group judged the risk here as medium rather than high. Full analytical detail is restricted to the CZ Hub. The risk picture has improved since a peace deal ended the Tigray conflict in November 2022, though airspace warnings remain in place. A new flare-up in fighting occurred in the Amhara region in February 2024.
HAAA.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: Improving airspace risk picture in Ethiopia's northern Tigray region (the Ethiopia/Eritrea border) since a peace deal was agreed in early Nov 2022. Airspace warnings remain in place — several states advise avoiding the area. The primary risk is from large-scale ceasefire violations involving missiles or anti-aircraft weaponry, which may present a risk to overflights through misidentification or crossfire. Ethiopia Airspace Update, July 2022 (OPSGROUP article) Major events: Feb 2024: New flare-up in fighting in the Amhara region (south of Tigray region), including air strikes. Nov 2022: Peace deal agreed in the Tigray region; Ethiopian Airlines planned to resume flights to HAMK/Mekele airport. Nov 2021: Several western countries issued airspace warnings and do-not-travel warnings for the Tigray region following increased fighting. July 2021: HAAA/Addis FIR published a NOTAM closing a section of airspace below FL290 over the Tigray following reports that militia shot down a military transport plane near the capital Mekele. Nov 2020: Major escalation of the conflict in the Tigray region. Some airways were closed by the Ethiopian and Sudanese CAAs. Airways UN321, UG300 and UL432 remained open but were very close to the conflict zone. Multiple airports were targeted by rockets; missiles were fired across the border into Eritrea targeting HHAS/Asmara, and HABD/Bahir Dar and HAGN/Gondar were also targeted. Sep 2018: Hidden ATC strike — Ethiopian ATC controllers went on strike and the ECAA and Ethiopian Airlines recruited retired and foreign controllers; many were not qualified to operate in Ethiopian airspace. The strike ended Sep 7.

VYYF.name: FIR Yangon, below FL260
VYYF.conflictType: Internal armed conflict — assessed by EASA as medium risk
VYYF.narrative: As with Ethiopia, this is a medium-risk Information Note rather than a do-not-operate CZIB. France's own national guidance goes slightly further operationally, setting a hard altitude floor. The security situation has deteriorated since the military coup in February 2021, with airstrikes and armed clashes across many parts of the country. GPS jamming has been reported on airway N895 and in the north of the FIR.
VYYF.restrictionLabel: Caution only — factor into your own risk assessment and routing, below FL 260

cross.detail: The security situation in Myanmar has deteriorated since the military coup in Feb 2021, with conflict and violence across many parts of the country involving air strikes and armed clashes. Several countries have issued airspace warnings at the lower flight levels due to the potential risk from military operations, surface-to-air fire and anti-aviation weaponry. GPS jamming (and possibly spoofing) has been reported in the north of the FIR for overflights between China and Bangladesh airspace. Major events: Jan 2024: Armed group shot down a military helicopter in the northern state of Kachin using a man-portable air-defence system (MANPAD). Sep 2023: Several attacks by rebel groups against military targets across the country, including a makeshift drone dropping bombs on aircraft hangars at an airbase next to VYNT/Naypyitaw airport. Sep 2023: Reports of intermittent GPS jamming on airway N895 over the mainland in the VYYF/Yangon FIR. Apr 2023: Myanmar's main airport VYYY/Yangon temporarily closed following an attack by resistance groups with improvised artillery rounds. Sep 2022: A Myanmar National Airlines passenger was reportedly shot as bullets passed through the fuselage of the ATR 72 aircraft on approach to VYLK/Loikaw. Feb 2021: Military coup ousted the government. ATC strike at the end of Feb resulted in no ATC service provided to overflights. Since then, there have been increasing strikes, mass protests, clashes with militia and airstrikes on areas where militia are active. OPSGROUP Article - Myanmar, Nov 2022
